question.prompt: A student recorded the exact percentage frequency distribution for a set of measurements, as shown below. However, the student neglected to indicate \(N,\) the total number of measurements. What is the smallest possible value of \(N?\) \[\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline \text{measured value} & \text{percent frequency}\\ \hline 0 & 12.5\\ \hline 1 & 0\\ \hline 2 & 50\\ \hline 3 & 25\\ \hline 4 & 12.5\\ \hline & 100\\ \hline\end{array}\]

solutions.explanation:
Each percentage must correspond to a whole number of measurements. Since
\[
12.5\%=\frac{12.5}{100}=\frac18,
\]
the number of measurements equal to \(0\) is \(N/8\). This must be a positive integer, so \(N\) must be a positive multiple of \(8\).

To check that \(8\) works for the entire distribution, take the counts of measured values \(0,1,2,3,4\) to be \(1,0,4,2,1\), respectively. These counts total \(8\) and give exactly the stated percentages. Therefore the smallest possible value is \(\boxed{8}\), choice B.
solutions.title: Use whole-number counts
